 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



The Effects of Repeated‑Sprint Training on Physical Fitness
and Physiological Adaptation in Athletes: A Systematic Review
and Meta‑Analysis
Fraser Thurlow1,2 · Minh Huynh3 · Andrew Townshend1,2 · Shaun J. McLaren4,5                · Lachlan P. James3    ·
Jonathon M. Taylor6 · Matthew Weston7 · Jonathon Weakley1,2,8

Accepted: 25 October 2023
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2023


Abstract
Background Repeated-sprint training (RST) is a common training method for enhancing physical fitness in athletes. To
advance RST prescription, it is important to understand the effects of programming variables on physical fitness and physi-
ological adaptation.
Objectives This study (1) quantifies the pooled effects of running RST on changes in 10 and 20 m sprint time, maximal
oxygen consumption (VO2max), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (YYIR1) distance, repeated-sprint ability (RSA),
countermovement jump (CMJ) height and change of direction (COD) ability in athletes, and (2) examines the moderating
effects of program duration, training frequency, weekly volume, sprint modality, repetition distance, number of repetitions
per set and number of sets per session on changes in these outcome measures.
Methods Pubmed, SPORTDiscus and Scopus databases were searched for original research articles up to 04 July 2023,
investigating RST in healthy, able-bodied athletes, between 14 and 35 years of age, and a performance calibre of trained
or above. RST interventions were limited to repeated, maximal running (land-based) sprints of ≤ 10 s duration, with ≤ 60 s
recovery, performed for 2–12 weeks. A Downs and Black checklist was used to assess the methodological quality of the
included studies. Eligible data were analysed using multi-level mixed-effects meta-analysis, with standardised mean changes
determined for all outcomes. Standardised effects [Hedges G (G)] were evaluated based on coverage of their confidence
(compatibility) intervals (CI) using a strength and conditioning specific reference value of G = 0.25 to declare an improvement
(i.e. G > 0.25) or impairment (i.e. G < − 0.25) in outcome measures. Applying the same analysis, the effects of programming
variables were then evaluated against a reference RST program, consisting of three sets of 6 × 30 m straight-line sprints
performed twice per week for 6 weeks (1200 m weekly volume).
Results 40 publications were included in our investigation, with data from 48 RST groups (541 athletes) and 19 active
control groups (213 athletes). Across all studies, the effects of RST were compatible with improvements in VO2max (G 0.56,
90% CI 0.32–0.80), YYIR1 distance (G 0.61, 90% CI 0.43–0.79), RSA decrement (G − 0.61, 90% CI − 0.85 to − 0.37),
linear sprint times (10 m: G − 0.35, 90% CI − 0.48 to − 0.22; 20 m: G − 0.48, 90% CI − 0.69 to − 0.27), RSA average time
(G − 0.34, 90% CI − 0.49 to − 0.18), CMJ height (G 0.26, 90% CI 0.13–0.39) and COD ability (G − 0.32, 90% CI − 0.52 to
− 0.12). Compared with the reference RST program, the effects of manipulating training frequency (+ 1 session per week),
program duration (+ 1 extra training week), RST volume (+ 200 m per week), number of reps (+ 2 per set), number of sets
per session (+ 1 set) or rep distance (+ 10 m per rep) were either non-substantial or comparable with an impairment in at
least one outcome measure per programming variable.
Conclusions Running-based RST improves speed, intermittent running performance, VO2max, RSA, COD ability and CMJ
height in trained athletes. Performing three sets of 6 × 30 m sprints, twice per week for 6 weeks is effective for enhancing
physical fitness and physiological adaptation. Additionally, since our findings do not provide conclusive support for the
manipulation of RST variables, further work is needed to better understand how programming factors can be manipulated
to augment training-induced adaptations.

 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Rugby"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective analysis (short communication) of official NRL match results from 2007 to 2019 (2,352 league matches, 4,704 team observations). For every 1,000 km of away travel, estimated win probability fell by 2.7% (95% CI -5.7 to 0.3%) and points difference by 1.1 points (95% CI -2.0 to -0.2), with the travel effect smaller in later seasons and no clear differences between states.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Travel was measured as straight-line distance from the away team's home stadium to the match venue, so actual route, time zones, and travel outside matches are not captured. The win-probability interval includes zero, so only the points-difference effect is clearly different from zero.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the 2.7% win-probability loss as a reliable per-trip effect for their own team, when the interval crosses zero and the figures are league-wide observational averages.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2022,
  "citation":"Read DB, Williams S, Fullagar HHK, Weakley JJS. The effects of travel on performance: a 13-year analysis of the National Rugby League (NRL) competition. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022;6(1):60-65.",
  "doi":"10.1080/24733938.2021.1876243",
  "abstract":"Analysis of 2,352 NRL matches (2007 to 2019) found that longer away travel was associated with a lower chance of winning and a smaller points difference. The effect of travel shrank over the 13 seasons, with no clear differences between states.",
  "tldr":"In the NRL, each 1,000 km of away travel was linked to a small drop in winning chances and in points margin. The effect has shrunk over time, but the win-probability estimate is imprecise.",
  "methods":"Exploratory retrospective analysis of official NRL match results from 2007 to 2019, excluding draws, play-offs and matches where a team played a home fixture outside its home city. Win or loss was modelled with a generalised linear mixed model and points difference with a linear mixed model, with team nested within season as a random effect and covariates for away disadvantage, turnaround time and opposition final ranking; travel was the straight-line distance from the away team's home stadium to the venue.",
  "findings":"Each 1,000 km of travel was associated with a 2.7% lower win probability (95% CI -5.7 to 0.3%) and a 1.1-point lower points difference (95% CI -2.0 to -0.2). Playing away had an odds ratio of 0.56 (0.48 to 0.66) for winning, and the travel effect was largest in 2007 to 2009 (-2.7%, 95% CI -4.7 to -0.6%) and close to zero in 2018 to 2019 (1.1%, 95% CI -1.2 to 3.3%).",
  "limitations":"Not all travel-related factors could be measured, travel outside matches was unknown, and no individual athlete measures were collected. The team's own ability was not modelled, and the single Victorian team (six titles in 13 seasons) showed no travel penalty, so the authors say a team-by-team analysis is needed.",
  "practicalImplications":"Coaches can estimate the likely effect of an away trip on match outcome and use it when planning travel logistics, sleeping arrangements and nutrition. The authors note that teams travelling more than 2,000 km for away matches could expect about 2.2 fewer points and a 5.4% lower winning likelihood on average.",
  "athleteDev":"Use the travel distance of an away fixture as a planning input for sleep, meals and logistics, because longer trips were linked to small average performance losses in this league. The study does not show that any specific travel strategy reduces those losses.",
  "rtp":"Does not inform return to sport: it analyses team match results for players in the competition, with no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play data."
 },

2	 "id":"Q85",
3	 "sourceFile":"The effects of velocity loss thresholds during resistance training on lower-limb performance enhancement - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf",
4	 "decision":"INCLUDE",
5	 "exclusionReason":"",
6	 "degradedReason":"",
7	 "doiMissing":false,
8	 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The effects of velocity loss thresholds during resistance training on lower-limb performance enhancement: A systematic review with meta-analysis' matches the filename.",
9	 "confidence":"high",
10	 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
11	 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
12	 "domains":["Training & Performance"],
13	 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
14	 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
15	 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
16	 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (308 participants, mostly men, aged about 14 to 24, with prior resistance training experience) comparing back-squat training with low (0 to 20%) and high (30 to 45%) velocity loss thresholds for 6 to 8 weeks. Within groups, both ranges improved 1RM, heavy-load and light-load squat velocity and CMJ height, while only low thresholds improved 20 m sprint time; between groups, heavy-load, light-load and sprint gains were larger with low thresholds (p < 0.05), and the CMJ difference was not significant (p = 0.088).",
17	 "screeningLimitations":"Only 13 studies were included, all 6 to 8 weeks long, squat-only, and with few CMJ or sprint training components. Allocation concealment was unclear in all studies, and the meta-regression used only linear-progression studies.",
18	 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the per-goal velocity loss ranges (Table 3) as settled prescriptions, when the interaction p values were 0.076 for CMJ and 0.010 for sprint and the CMJ between-group result was not significant.",
19	 "paper":{
20	  "year":2024,
21	  "citation":"Chen BY, et al. The effects of velocity loss thresholds during resistance training on lower-limb performance enhancement: A systematic review with meta-analysis. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024:1-15.",
22	  "doi":"10.1177/17479541241244581",
23	  "abstract":"Meta-analysis of 13 studies (308 participants) of back-squat training with low (0 to 20%) or high (30 to 45%) velocity loss thresholds. Low thresholds gave larger heavy-load squat velocity, light-load squat velocity and sprint gains, while maximal strength gains were similar between thresholds.",
24	  "tldr":"Squat sets stopped at about 20% velocity loss gave better speed and power gains than sets allowed to lose 30 to 45%, while maximal strength changed similarly. Coaches may prefer low thresholds when speed or power is the goal.",
25	  "methods":"PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021247929) of five databases searched in May 2023. Included peer-reviewed randomised trials of back-squat training of at least 4 weeks that used velocity monitoring and ended sets at a set velocity loss threshold; effects were pooled as Hedges g with random-effects models, and meta-regression was run on linear-progression studies only.",
26	  "findings":"Between-group differences favoured low thresholds for heavy-load squat velocity (ES -0.40, p = 0.005), light-load squat velocity (ES -0.39, p = 0.025) and sprint time (ES -0.47, p = 0.022). The CMJ difference (ES -0.24, p = 0.088) and 1RM difference (ES -0.65, p = 0.630) were not significant.",
27	  "limitations":"The abstract and discussion describe the CMJ advantage of low thresholds as superior although p = 0.088, which is not significant. The sprint meta-regression p value is 0.010 in the abstract and discussion but 0.002 in the results. High-threshold group labels also vary between 30 to 40% and 30 to 45% across the text and figures, and the studies were short, squat-only programs.",
28	  "practicalImplications":"For speed or jump goals, stopping sets at about 10 to 20% velocity loss is the best-supported range, with sprint gains most consistent at 10% or less. For maximal strength alone, a 0 to 40% range gave similar gains in the authors' table, so tight control may not be needed.",
29	  "athleteDev":"Use a velocity loss of 20% or less on squat sets when the goal is speed, power or jump height, and 10% or less when sprint time is the priority. Strength-only blocks can tolerate wider thresholds, but the review did not test these over a full training season.",
30	  "rtp":"Cannot inform return to sport: all included trials used healthy, non-injured, resistance-trained people, and no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes were assessed."
31	 }
32	}

Abstract
This study assessed the effects of squat training with different velocity loss (VL) thresholds on squat strength, heavy-load
squat velocity (HLSV), light-load squat velocity (LLSV), countermovement jump (CMJ) height, and sprint time (ST). A sys-
tematic search of electronic databases was conducted. Meta-analysis was used to examine effects of trainings with differ-
ent VL thresholds and used meta-regression to examine the interaction effects (correlation) between training effects and
VL in different performance-based outcomes. Our systematic search yielded 1017 articles, 13 of which were included in
the present study. Meta-analysis revealed that resistance training with both low (0%–20%) and high (30%–45%) VL thresh-
olds improved squat strength, HLSV, LLSV, and CMJ height, but only low VL improved ST (p < 0.05). Training gains for
HLSV, LLSV, CMJ (p = 0.088), and ST with low VL were superior to those with high VL (p < 0.05). Meta-regression
revealed that CMJ (p = 0.076) and ST (p = 0.010) demonstrated improvements as VL decreased in the range of 0% to
45%. In conclusion, squat resistance training with low (≤20%) VL provides relatively more effective training stimuli,
improving performance in power and speed tasks. Optimal VL ranges may be in the range 10% to 20%, ≤20%, and
≤10% for the HLSV and LLSV, CMJ, and ST, respectively.

Acupuncture gave short-term carpal tunnel and low back pain benefit, while its performance evidence was conflicting.",

28	  "practicalImplications":"The review supports trying Kinesio tape before activity for athletes with acute shoulder symptoms, with the expectation of a small, short-lived effect. 29	  "athleteDev":"Kinesio tape is a low-cost option for athletes with shoulder symptoms before activity, but do not expect it to change strength or sprint performance. The review found no firm support for massage or acupuncture as performance aids.",

 "id":"Q86",
 "sourceFile":"The evidence for common nonsurgical modalities in sports medicine, Part 1 - Kinesio tape, sports massage therapy, and acupuncture.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Evidence for Common Nonsurgical Modalities in Sports Medicine, Part 1: Kinesio Tape, Sports Massage Therapy, and Acupuncture' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Review article of publications from 2006 to 2019 found through PubMed and Google Scholar on Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture. The authors report low-level evidence for a small, short-term pain and range-of-motion effect of Kinesio tape (suggested for athletes with acute shoulder symptoms before activity), acupuncture for carpal tunnel syndrome and as an adjunct for low back pain, and little or conflicting evidence for sports massage or acupuncture effects on performance.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The method is described only as PubMed and Google Scholar searches with no search terms, eligibility criteria or appraisal method, so it is a narrative review rather than a systematic one. Most cited trials are small, with short follow-up and limited blinding.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the performance section as evidence that taping, massage or acupuncture improves athletic performance, when the authors found little, small or conflicting evidence for performance outcomes.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2020,
  "citation":"Trofa DP, Obana KK, Herndon CL, Noticewala MS, Parisien RL, Popkin CA, et al. The Evidence for Common Nonsurgical Modalities in Sports Medicine, Part 1: Kinesio Tape, Sports Massage Therapy, and Acupuncture. JAAOS Glob Res Rev. 2020;4(1):e19.00104.",
  "doi":"10.5435/JAAOSGlobal-D-19-00104",
  "abstract":"Narrative review of Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture in athletes and patients with musculoskeletal conditions, drawn from publications from 2006 to 2019. The evidence is low-level, with small, short-term effects for some uses and little evidence for sports performance.",
  "tldr":"Kinesio tape may be reasonable for athletes with shoulder symptoms before activity, but the benefit is small and short-term. Acupuncture has some support for carpal tunnel syndrome and as a low back pain adjunct, and evidence for sports massage and performance is weak.",
  "methods":"Narrative review of publications from 2006 to 2019 found through PubMed and Google Scholar, covering three modalities: Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture. No search terms, eligibility criteria or risk-of-bias method are reported.",
  "findings":"Kinesio tape trials showed short-term pain or range-of-motion changes, with no sustained benefit and conflicting strength results. For sports massage, a meta-analysis cited by the authors found immediate benefit for shoulder and neck pain but short-term benefit for shoulder pain only, and performance results were mixed (one study found higher jump height and less soreness, another no change in sprint speed). Acupuncture gave short-term carpal tunnel and adjunct low back pain benefit, while its performance evidence was conflicting.",
  "limitations":"The method is described only as a PubMed and Google Scholar search, so coverage is unknown and selection cannot be checked. The authors repeatedly note low-quality trials with short follow-up and limited blinding, and two authors disclose financial relationships with Arthrex, Smith and Nephew, and Stryker.",
  "practicalImplications":"The review supports trying Kinesio tape before activity for athletes with acute shoulder symptoms, with the expectation of a small, short-lived effect. Acupuncture can be considered as an adjunct for low back pain or carpal tunnel symptoms, and the authors say massage needs higher quality research before firm recommendations.",
  "athleteDev":"Kinesio tape is a low-cost option for athletes with shoulder symptoms before activity, but do not expect it to change strength or sprint performance. The review found no firm support for massage or acupuncture as performance aids.",
  "rtp":"Partly relevant: the review covers shoulder symptoms and low back pain, but it gives no return-to-play criteria or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot set return-to-sport timing."
 },
 "verification":{
  "status":"CORRECTED",
  "changes":[
   "paper.findings: massage gave 'short-term shoulder and neck pain relief' -> immediate effects for both, short-term for shoulder only (\"immediate positive effects of massage therapy on both shoulder and neck pain with short-term positive effects for shoulder pain only\")",
   "paper.limitations: 'several authors disclose' -> two authors (Dr. Ahmad and Dr. Popkin); 'most trials small, unblinded' softened to what the authors state",
   "paper.practicalImplications: 'sports massage for short-term symptom relief' recommendation not made by authors -> \"There is a need for higher quality research to better elucidate the effect of sports massage therapy\"",
   "paper.citation: only first author listed -> first six authors plus et al."
  ],
  "residualConcerns":"",
  "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

  "findings":"Kinesio tape trials showed short-term pain or range-of-motion changes, with no sustained benefit and conflicting strength results. For sports massage, a meta-analysis cited by the authors found immediate benefit for shoulder and neck pain but short-term benefit for shoulder pain only, and performance results were mixed (one study found higher jump height and less soreness, another no change in sprint speed).   "limitations":"The method is described only as a PubMed and Google Scholar search, so coverage is unknown and selection cannot be checked.   "abstract":"Narrative review of cupping and blood flow restriction (BFR) training in athletes and patients.   "tldr":"Dry cupping may be reasonable for nonspecific neck, back or shoulder pain, and low-load BFR may build strength and endurance when cuff pressure is controlled. Evidence is limited, and a performance benefit for athletes is not established.",

  "practicalImplications":"Dry cupping can be considered as an adjunct for interested athletes with neck, back or shoulder pain, since the authors judge the risk low when it is done properly.    ABSTRACT   ARTICLE HISTORY
   Background: Chronic alcohol misuse is associated with alcoholic myopathy, characterized by   Received 14 July 2021
   skeletal muscle weakness and atrophy. Moreover, there is evidence that sports-related people   Revised 1 February 2022
   seem to exhibit a greater prevalence of problematic alcohol consumption, especially binge drinking   Accepted 8 February 2022
   (BD), which might not cause alcoholic myopathy but can negatively impact muscle function and   KEYWORDS
   amateur and professional athletic performance.   Alcohol; alcoholic myopathy;
   Objective: To review the literature concerning the effects of alcohol consumption on skeletal muscle   muscle performance;
   function and structure that can affect muscle performance.   problematic alcohol
   Methodology: We examined the currently available literature (PubMed, Google Scholars) to develop   consumption; muscle
   a narrative review summarizing the knowledge about the effects of alcohol on skeletal muscle function   pathology; binge drinking
   and exercise performance, obtained from studies in human beings and animal models for problematic
   alcohol consumption.
   Results: Exercise- and sport-based studies indicate that alcohol consumption can negatively affect
   muscle recovery after vigorous exercise, especially in men, while women seem less affected. Clinical
   studies and pre-clinical laboratory research have led to the knowledge of some of the mechanisms
   involved in alcohol-related muscle dysfunction, including an imbalance between anabolic and
   catabolic pathways, reduced regeneration, increased inflammation and fibrosis, and deficiencies
   in energetic balance and mitochondrial function. These pathological features can appear not only
   under chronic alcohol misuse but also in other alcohol consumption patterns.
   Conclusions: Most laboratory-based studies use chronic or acute alcohol exposure, while episodic
   BD, the most common drinking pattern in amateur and professional athletes, is underrepresented.
   Nevertheless, alcohol consumption negatively affects skeletal muscle health through different
   mechanisms, which collectively might contribute to reduced sports performance.
   RESUMEN
   Introduccion: El consumo crónico del alcohol se ha asociado al desarrollo de la miopatía alcohólica,
   una condición del músculo esquelético que se caracteriza por debilitamiento muscular y atrofia. Por
   otro lado, la evidencia sugiere que existe una alta prevalencia del consumo problemático de alcohol
   en deportistas, lo que ocurre principalmente en un patrón por atracón (Binge Drinking, BD, en ingles)
   y que puede impactar negativamente la funcion muscular, y por lo tanto, el desempeño deportivo.
   Objetivo: Revisar en la literatura los efectos del consumo del alcohol en la estructura y función
   del músculo esquelético que podrían afectar el rendimiento deportivo.
   Metodología: Se realizó una revisión de la literatura actualizada, desarrollando un artículo narrativo
   sobre el consumo del alcohol en la función del músculo esquelético y el rendimiento en el ejercicio,
   que recopila conocimientos obtenidos de estudios en humanos y modelos animales de consumo
   problemático del alcohol.
   Resultados: Los estudios basados en deporte y ejercicio sugieren que el consumo de alcohol afecta
   negativamente la recuperación del músculo esquelético luego de un ejercicio vigoroso, especialmente
   en hombres, mientras que las mujeres se parecen menos afectadas. Por otro lado, estudios clínicos y pre-
   clínicos han permitido conocer algunos de los mecanismos involucrados en la disfunción muscular
   ocasionada por el alcohol, los que incluyen un desbalance entre las vías anabólicas y catabólicas,
   regeneración deficiente, un aumento en la inflamación y fibrosis, y desbalances en el equilibrio
   energético y la función mitocondrial. Estos mecanismos patológicos pueden ocurrir no solo en el

   ABSTRACT   ARTICLE HISTORY
   Background: Chronic alcohol misuse is associated with alcoholic myopathy, characterized by   Received 14 July 2021
   skeletal muscle weakness and atrophy. Moreover, there is evidence that sports-related people   Revised 1 February 2022
   seem to exhibit a greater prevalence of problematic alcohol consumption, especially binge drinking   Accepted 8 February 2022
   (BD), which might not cause alcoholic myopathy but can negatively impact muscle function and   KEYWORDS
   amateur and professional athletic performance.   Alcohol; alcoholic myopathy;
   Objective: To review the literature concerning the effects of alcohol consumption on skeletal muscle   muscle performance;
   function and structure that can affect muscle performance.   problematic alcohol
   Methodology: We examined the currently available literature (PubMed, Google Scholars) to develop   consumption; muscle
   a narrative review summarizing the knowledge about the effects of alcohol on skeletal muscle function   pathology; binge drinking
   and exercise performance, obtained from studies in human beings and animal models for problematic
   alcohol consumption.
   Results: Exercise- and sport-based studies indicate that alcohol consumption can negatively affect
   muscle recovery after vigorous exercise, especially in men, while women seem less affected. Clinical
   studies and pre-clinical laboratory research have led to the knowledge of some of the mechanisms
   involved in alcohol-related muscle dysfunction, including an imbalance between anabolic and
   catabolic pathways, reduced regeneration, increased inflammation and fibrosis, and deficiencies
   in energetic balance and mitochondrial function. These pathological features can appear not only
   under chronic alcohol misuse but also in other alcohol consumption patterns.
   Conclusions: Most laboratory-based studies use chronic or acute alcohol exposure, while episodic
   BD, the most common drinking pattern in amateur and professional athletes, is underrepresented.
   Nevertheless, alcohol consumption negatively affects skeletal muscle health through different
   mechanisms, which collectively might contribute to reduced sports performance.
   RESUMEN
   Introduccion: El consumo crónico del alcohol se ha asociado al desarrollo de la miopatía alcohólica,
   una condición del músculo esquelético que se caracteriza por debilitamiento muscular y atrofia. Por
   otro lado, la evidencia sugiere que existe una alta prevalencia del consumo problemático de alcohol
   en deportistas, lo que ocurre principalmente en un patrón por atracón (Binge Drinking, BD, en ingles)
   y que puede impactar negativamente la funcion muscular, y por lo tanto, el desempeño deportivo.
   Objetivo: Revisar en la literatura los efectos del consumo del alcohol en la estructura y función
   del músculo esquelético que podrían afectar el rendimiento deportivo.
   Metodología: Se realizó una revisión de la literatura actualizada, desarrollando un artículo narrativo
   sobre el consumo del alcohol en la función del músculo esquelético y el rendimiento en el ejercicio,
   que recopila conocimientos obtenidos de estudios en humanos y modelos animales de consumo
   problemático del alcohol.
   Resultados: Los estudios basados en deporte y ejercicio sugieren que el consumo de alcohol afecta
   negativamente la recuperación del músculo esquelético luego de un ejercicio vigoroso, especialmente
   en hombres, mientras que las mujeres se parecen menos afectadas. Por otro lado, estudios clínicos y pre-
   clínicos han permitido conocer algunos de los mecanismos involucrados en la disfunción muscular
   ocasionada por el alcohol, los que incluyen un desbalance entre las vías anabólicas y catabólicas,
   regeneración deficiente, un aumento en la inflamación y fibrosis, y desbalances en el equilibrio
   energético y la función mitocondrial. Estos mecanismos patológicos pueden ocurrir no solo en el

   Conclusiones: La mayoría de las investigaciones se han concentrado en evaluar los efectos de la
   exposición a alcohol aguda o crónica en el músculo esquelético, mientras que el BD, el patrón de
   consumo más común y frecuente en deportistas aficionados y profesionales ha sido poco estudiado. No
   obstante, el consumo de alcohol afecta negativamente la salud del músculo esquelético a través de
   mecanismos que podrían contribuir a reducir el rendimiento deportivo.

 "screeningLimitations":"The search is described only as PubMed and Google Scholar with no systematic method, so coverage is unknown. Most mechanistic evidence comes from animals, cell cultures and patients with chronic alcohol misuse rather than athletes, and binge drinking is underrepresented.",

  "abstract":"Narrative review of alcohol effects on skeletal muscle in humans, animal models and cell studies, with a focus on sportspeople. Acute and chronic alcohol impair recovery and muscle function through mechanisms that may reduce athletic performance, but binge drinking is understudied.",

  "methods":"Narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar literature on alcohol and skeletal muscle in humans and animal models, covering acute and chronic exposure, sex differences and molecular mechanisms. The authors summarise human exercise-recovery findings by dose and sex in a single figure.",
  "findings":"Acute alcohol after eccentric exercise increased muscle damage and impaired strength recovery in young men at about 1.0 g/kg, but not at 0.5 g/kg or when the exercise was a task participants were trained for; the doses tested in women (0.8 g/kg body mass, 0.88 and 1.09 g/kg lean mass) did not change recovery. Chronic alcohol reduces anabolic signalling and regeneration, and raises inflammation, fibrosis, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in animal and clinical studies.",
  "limitations":"Most human studies used a single acute dose in a controlled laboratory, and binge patterns, which are common among athletes, are underrepresented. The review gives no search protocol, and the sport-specific data are small and split by sex.",
  "practicalImplications":"Athletes can be told that heavy drinking after hard, unaccustomed eccentric sessions may increase muscle damage and slow strength recovery, particularly in men. The review does not show how repeated binge drinking affects training adaptation, so the acute findings should not be assumed to carry over.",
  "athleteDev":"After heavy or muscle-damaging sessions, advise athletes that alcohol at around 1 g/kg may lengthen strength recovery. The review does not give safe intake thresholds for athletes.",
  "rtp":"Partly relevant: alcohol after eccentric exercise damage slowed strength recovery in the cited work, but the review includes no injured athletes or return-to-sport tests and cannot set return-to-play timing."

   "paper.practicalImplications: 'prolong muscle soreness' not stated for men -> increased muscle damage and slowed strength recovery (\"alcohol intake enhanced muscle injury and retarded the recovery of skeletal muscle strength\")",
   "paper.athleteDev: removed generic 'plan recovery days around heavy nights out' advice; tied to the dose studied"
  ],
  "residualConcerns":"No volume, issue or pages are printed (online-first, published online 07 Apr 2022).",
  "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}
